projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with John Medynski was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of John J. Medynski. Mr. Medynski is a veteran of World War II, Korea, and Vietnam. John served in the Navy aboard several ships and he was also involved in atomic testing in the '50s. I'm Tom Swope, and this phone interview was recorded on June 30th, 2002. John was 79 at the time of this recording. Where were you living when the war started?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh, boy. Okay. Where were you living when the war started?

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: I was living in Wisconsin in the little village of Lublin.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh. And were you drafted?

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: I was drafted. And when I was drafted, they gave me a choice of going to the Army or Navy, and I chose the Navy.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Why did you choose the Navy?

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: I don't know. I guess it was that furthest thing away. From the water, I thought I wanted to go in the Navy. Anyway, prior to that, I had just applied for the Maritime Service Academy, but I didn't hear anything from them. So when I got drafted, I went to the Navy. And I was in the Navy in boot camp in Great Lakes two weeks when I got a notice that I was accepted for the Maritime Academy, but it was a little bit late by then. But I guess I was lucky, because a lot of Maritime ships went down.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So when -- so when exactly did you go in?

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: I went in March the 3rd, 1943.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: '43. Do you have any memories of the day the Japanese attacked Pearl Harbor?

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: No, that -- except that radio --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: -- from Roosevelt.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Would you remember being at home and hearing that?

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: Yeah, I wasn't at -- at that time, yes, I was at home and heard it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: And I guess that's one of the reasons I wanted to go in the Navy. I don't know why.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: All right. Tell me whatever you can about your training then.

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: My training?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: I went to boot camp in Great Lakes. It was a brand new camp. It was called Green Bay. And we had to march through the mud all the time. And at that time and while I was in the -- in the boot camp, I acquired some of the baby diseases like scarlet fever and whooping cough. Not whooping cough, but German measles. That kept me in the sick bay for a little while, so I missed out on some of the activities, but -- like rowing boats on Lake Michigan, which I didn't think was very good.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: So -- but they didn't ship -- didn't extend my time at boot camp. I went out of there in -- in June. And then I went to -- from there, I went to Auburn, Alabama, for the radio school.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: They chose -- chose radio, because at that time I had a little bit of experience in radio communications, because I went to the program prior to my drafting, under the YMCA, which was called "War Workers Program."

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: And it was radio communications, so I knew the code and that by the time I got drafted.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So that was your job then; you were radioman?

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: Yes, sir.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh. What was your first ship?

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: My first ship was the USS Cole. Not the one that got blown up here, but an old 1919 four-stacker destroyer that was converted to a three-stack. And it was one of -- it was supposedly one of the fastest ships at that time. Not including the carriers and that, but --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And --

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: I mean, it was -- some of the experiences I wrote you about was on that first ship.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh. So when -- when did you go on the Cole then? That was late in '43?

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: Pardon me?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You went on the Cole late in '43 then, 1943?

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: Yes. No, in early '44.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Early '44.

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: Because I went from radio school. I went up to Portland, Maine, Casco Bay, and went to High Direction Finder School, which is where we used to listen to -- used to listen to submarine broadcasts and try and get a fix on them. I think I wrote to you about that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: And I spent on the Cole until 19 -- November of 1945; which, at that time, I was eligible to get out, because I got married in the meantime and I was eligible to get out of the service. I got out of the service. But soon after I got out of the service -- the reason I got -- supposedly got -- went and got married was, I had supposedly gotten this woman pregnant. But when I got home from the service, she was no longer pregnant. I heard that she got an abortion, so I divorced her. But after that, I stayed out of the service a little over a year and then went back in. I went out as a second-class radioman and I come back in as a third-class. And I went aboard the Juneau from there; which, I sent you a web page.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah, I've got that right in front of me, as a matter of fact.

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: The Juneau, spent four years on that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Getting back to World War II, you took the Cole overseas then? You went --

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: -- overseas on the Cole?

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: Yeah, we went several small trips, convoy duty for the supply ships. They would send supplies down to the Caribbean, like Cuba and Jamaica and Recife Brazilo, which is now part of ?Buco de Reef? And we would escort these ships down there. And these were supplies for the seaplane at the airfield -- airports with seaports.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: And then we went on couple convoys to the Atlantic, which I think I mentioned one of them in -- in the journal.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah. Why don't you go ahead and tell me that again, any -- any memorable convoys that you can remember.

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: On that journey?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh. Yes.

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: On that trip?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: Well, most of the time, we were -- we would be going with the convoy. And every -- and every evening, the commander of the convoy would come up on the radio and tell us this is the situation; on the voice radio. And it was -- at that time, it wasn't encrypted or anything, so anybody could pick it up. And we -- we would -- my duty at that time was on the high direction finder where we would try and get -- listen to the -- during our period on watch, we'd listen for submarine broadcasts and we'd tried to get a bearing on them. And there were other ships doing the same thing, trying to get a bearing on a trans -- on the transmission. And then they would send somebody out to drop depth charges. And we went out several times and did chases dropping depth charges over, but I never had -- don't know if we ever hit one or not --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: -- or sunk one.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you lose any ships on any of those convoys to U-boats?

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: They -- yeah, on that convoy that we took to -- to Casablanca, before we got into the -- the -- what they call it, what canal that is.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Straits --

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: Gibraltar.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: -- of Gibraltar? Right.

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: Gibraltar. Every evening -- every -- just about every evening, we'd have -- the submarines at that time were pretty thick and they would be, you know, blowing up them ships. And if an ammunition ship would blow up, that's all you seen was a big ball of fire. And after -- that convoy started off with 100 ships, not counting -- I believe it wasn't counting the escorts itself, which were those small, little Jeep carrier --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: -- and the destroyers and destroyer escorts. And when we -- when we arrived, there was only 20 ships -- 26 ships left out of that convoy. The rest was sunk.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Wow. Wow.

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: They would be picking up survivors every so often.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: But that's -- that's what I was told. Now, I -- I witnessed some of the explosions of the ammo ships and that, because that was in the night.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh. Did you -- what was life like on the ship?

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: Pardon me?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was your life like on that ship?

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: Life like?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah, your life on the ship.

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: Pretty bad. Anyway, when -- we would get fresh food when we'd first report. In two weeks, we didn't have any more -- no -- no fresh milk, no meat, no -- all they had was a bin of potatoes that might last a little while. And that was all decked in with screened-in containers that carried it. We had powdered eggs, powdered milk, little beef, that canned beef, and any Spam and stuff. And then when we -- we lived in the afterquarters, which was called the guinea pool -- the guinea pool got pretty bad. We had to go topside on the main deck to get anywhere out of that compartment. And in that compartment was the -- the bunks were three high. They were just metal tubing frame with the canvas stretched out, and then they had a thin mattress on top of that which had a hard, rubber-type cover so it wouldn't burn very easily. We could open -- open that. And then we carried our own bedding and that at that time from the beginning, your mattress, your -- your blankets, your pillow, and, you know, sea -- then we'd wrap that, roll it up, and wrap it around the sea bag, which sea bag is where we kept all our carryout clothing whenever we went anywhere. So you had to haul that around from place to place when we got transferred. But on that ship, the food was brought in from the galley in tureens, which are little containers, wherever the cooks were. Then we would eat -- eat in the regular same living quarters. They would have a table which was usually secured in the overhead or ceiling. And the lower-down benches would be -- one side was benches and the other side they used for seats of the table was the lockers which was just below the bunks. Bunks could be folded against the bulkhead or wall, whatever you want to call it, ship. And we would eat there and then the mess cooks would bring -- would take and clear it up and haul it back, clean everything up, and stow the tables up. And if we wanted to go to the bathroom, we would have to go up the ladder top side and then on a -- go off the back end. The fantail of the ship was the -- was the head or the toilet. And under the toilets had just a trough where the water was steadily -- sea water was steadily being pumped in forward part of that -- of that head. And those are the troughs out and back down into the ocean. And you had seats. You know, you sat on those seats and do our thing.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: And they also had a urinal, two urinals, one on each side that you could use. But the bathing facilities, you did not have hot water and such. We would use saltwater line. And it had a -- two valves that you could mix saltwater and steam and get warm water that way. And you used saltwater soap, which was a big bar of yellow-looking soap, and with salt, washed down with that. And then after we finished washing, to rinse ourselves off of that saltwater, we would draw a bucket of freshwater with a different tap. And we'd only use about two gallons of water to rinse ourselves off with that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: We could heat it with the steam line so it could be warm and -- but -- but they had some -- it was always pretty rough on that little small destroyer.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: And ?you would Branock? If you had to go from the compartment to the radio shack, which was all the way forward, you had to walk on the main deck. And if the weather was rough, they would put out a -- a high line or a line, stretch it out and with little rings on it like you see on some of the street cars. And probably you'd hang on, but this was on a line. You'd drag this thing and go like hell if you could make it to the radio shack before some wave hit you. And you'd try to time it so you could make it. Every once in a while you wouldn't make it and you'd get hit with sea water. And you'd better hang on. And that was about it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you have a chance to do anything for entertainment on the ship?

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: For -- for entertainment?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: The only entertainment we had was whatever we could find to play cards or something. The radiomen didn't have it too bad because we could get some broadcasts once in a while, like BBC or something like that, and listen to it. But other than that, we didn't have nothing -- we would copy some code, press news, for the crew and pass it out. But as far as -- they'd have entertainment. They'd show movies. If the weather was good enough, they would show movies up on forward deck. And that's about it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you have any memories of buddies onboard the Cole?

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: Memories of what?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Buddies, friends.

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: Oh, friends.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: Oh, I remember some of them. Not too much of them now. My memory is pretty well gone. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When you think of --

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: Some of the radiomen, but I never stayed in contact with them, with anyone.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: I guess I was a loner.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah. When you think of the World War II years, does any particularly vivid memory come to mind?

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: No, I didn't have any particular memory.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: Just that it was boring and that there was nothing to do.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: Played cards.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So next, it was the Juneau, right? That was the --

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You were on the Juneau during the Korean War?

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: During Korean War, yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh. And where were you --

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: I went, I think, right after World War II. I was there -- I was on there from 1948 to 1952.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: Was on the Juneau. We went on a couple Sixth Fleet Mediterranean cruises, which was really nice to visit a lot of seaports. The ship was a good-looking ship and everybody would come visit us.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: Then during the Korean War, we went -- we were first U.S. vessel to fire on the Korean coast, gunfire support for the Army. And we stayed out on that particular mission in Korea for a full year. Got what they call a homeward bound panic, because we were gone a year.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you ever go ashore in Korea?

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: Not in Korea, no. We would go to Japan, then get the ammunition back and we'd go ashore in Japan a couple of times. And then for three months, we were a communications ship in Taiwan, in Keelung, a little town in Taiwan -- a little town in Taiwan -- for three months out of that period. So we went ashore there, but there was nothing to do there but see the -- walk around and see their caves that they had developed.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah. Tell me about those.

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: Well, they would have big -- in the side of mountains, they would have -- they would have carved out big caves. They would drive trucks in them. They'd store equipment and everything else they could have. And they had radar and everything else up top so they could find out, see whatever they were using. Radio communications under there, under -- in there. They had pretty elaborate caves. And this was all done by carving out with a hammer and chisel, then, you know, hauled it out of there. Probably used some air that they had times to where they could reach it, but -- The Japanese had particular -- had the same similar to that in Yokuska, but that was after -- after the war that we visited Japan that we -- I went through their caves. But they're like two stories of caves. Very big complexes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And what kinds of things were they planning on storing in those caves in Japan?

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: Well, they -- I guess it was safe from bombardments and they could hide their equipment so nobody'd see it and things like that. That's all I know of. I would say it's mainly to protect from any bombs that somebody might drop.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you have any other strong memories of Korea?

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: Well, let's see. Korea, not -- not that -- not much except that we did do a lot of firing for the first -- in the first week that we were firing, we emptied every shell we had. And we were a -- what they called an anti-aircraft cruiser, which had a lot of ammunition to fire. And we used it all up and had to go back to Sasebo in Japan and load up and -- and fire again. But we did a lot of firing. And we would stand watches four hours on, four hours off. And in the four hours off, you had to shave, bathe, eat and do whatever you wanted to do, and then go back on watch again. So that lasted about five months. And it was tiresome. You didn't get much sleep.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah. Now, were you involved -- after Korea, were you involved in the atomic testing, atomic bomb testing?

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: Yes, in 1958 in the ?Bikini enemy retook area? I was transferred to a fleet tug, which is a big seagoing tug, and I was a radioman aboard there. And then we would put out test arrays, which the ship would put out test arrays for the tests all around it, bomb sites. And then after the explosion and bomb, when it got safe enough to go, supposedly safe enough to go in there, we'd take those test arrays and read them and like tape-recorders and things like that. And they would -- they would read them. And we did that -- I figured I got a lot of information on that. There was something like 26 bombs that they set off. Some mega -- some big ones and others were small. Underwater blasts and surface blasts and air blasts. It was pretty spectacular as far as the sights are concerned.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So did you actually observe them, actually look at them as they exploded?

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: Pardon me?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were you observing them? Did -- you were watching the explosions?

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: Yeah, we could watch them because we used to get one of these little thick glasses, wear these glasses like the weld -- almost like welders use. And -- and you couldn't see anything until -- but when a blast would go off, it seemed like it was bright daylight, even with the glasses on. And there was some -- I think I sent you a web page on that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: And there was some conversation that some of the men seen -- they said they would have their -- they would be sitting on the opposite side of the ship and they could -- when the blast went off, they had their heads -- arms below their eyes and that, and they said they could see -- it looked like x-rays. They could see the bones. But I never witnessed that. I don't know. But that's what some of the men had written letters to this outfit and said that was their experience.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: We'd wash down the ship after we'd come back from the blast site and all that. But it was -- it was pretty spectacular as far as -- well, that underwater one is really the one that -- because they had all kinds of ships anchored all over the area, aircraft carriers and old destroyers. And they had a submarine that was submerged there. And when that thing went off, you seen a plume of water go up. And then as it come down, it would roll out. And pretty soon all the ships, you couldn't see them. They're all covered with that water. And after a while when it settled down, you could see that some of the ships had sunk, they were gone. But it was -- you could -- we were close enough where we could see all this.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Wow. And you were involved in 26 of these that you were part of?

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: Pardon me?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you say you were part of 26 of these tests?

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: We were there -- we were there from, I think it was, March through August. March, April, May. Nine -- nine months, I believe, all together.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: There was a lot of tests. Some of them were -- it was about five or six megatons. But you weren't very close to those. We were -- I know they were saying that we were seven miles away from one. It was really dark in the morning. And when it went off, it was just like broad summer daylight, sunshine outside.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: Just that bright. Seven miles away.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you suffer any effects from being that close?

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: Not that I know of. I -- but sometime the doc told me I had liver spots or something. I don't know. But I have -- I haven't got any leukemia or anything like that, that I know of. And my health seems to be good, so I -- I had some -- I got a record of what dosage I had during the period of time that we were there. But other than that, my health -- I had -- I had an enlarged thyroid which I was treated for and it's -- it's went down all right. But I don't know if that was due to any of that radiation or not.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: But there -- there was radiation, because we towed three destroyers on the site that were in the test itself. We took -- dropped off two in Honolulu and one in San Francisco. That took about a month to get to San Francisco. And when we got there, they checked us with Geiger counters. And you could still hear the increase of -- of the clicks on that Geiger counter around the shoes and that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: So we did have some radiation.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh. Now, you mentioned your hearing. Did you say that was a result of something that you had gone through when you were in the Navy?

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: What was that again?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Your hearing. You said your hearing. Was that was affected by your Navy --

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Yeah, that, I got a disability for Navy -- it was a service disability for hearing. And mainly because the radio, because you copied -- copied code continually and it was -- sometimes the signals were pretty low and you had to turn the volume up and -- and there was always static. And at that time, the communication isn't like it is today. You copied code and you'd wear earphones on the radio.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: But now the teletype takes care of everything, computer.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So just wearing those headphones so much, right?

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: Well, the noise.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: The actually having them hours and hours of noise beating on your ears --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: -- I guess. And then when we went, the ships aren't too quiet. There's noise there, so --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Any other memories of the atomic testing that you can think of?

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: No, not -- not that's nothing special.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh. Now, you were also involved --

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: Oh, there is one -- one incident that I can remember that seemed odd. When we would go to the site after the bomb went off, after supposedly coast was clear enough to go in, it seemed like there was a dividing line on the -- on the ocean. The one side would be a little rough. And then after just -- then another part would be real smooth. And they said -- they told me that that was due to some of the radiation or something. There was just a real, real fine line that you could see where the difference was, where the -- where some of the -- I guess where the water from the shock or something met the other.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: That's the only thing I can think of. But I noticed that it was that way.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: I think I had a letter I wrote in that -- to that outfit on that page that I sent you.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right. Exactly. Now, you were also involved in -- in Vietnam, right?

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: Yes, we were.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Okay. Tell me about that.

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: Most of it was just we would be on -- I was on a guided missile destroyer at that time and we didn't have any instruments. We would be mostly on guard for the carriers. We'd go floating back and forth. The carriers would do bombing and all that. That -- that was just a monotonous period. It was months and months of same thing, going back and forth with the carriers while they were taking off and bombing the coast. We didn't -- we didn't go ashore anywhere. And at one time, we'd be -- we had a Marine detachment aboard and the Marines went in one night just to -- with rubber boat -- to blow up a railroad tunnel. And that's about it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh. What was the name of that destroyer?

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: Pardon me?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was the name of that ship?

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: I can't hear you.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: The name of the ship that you were on in Vietnam.

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: The name of the ship was the Cochrane.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: DDG-21.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: C-o-c-h-r-a-n-e.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Now, which ship were you on when you were doing the atomic testing?

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: That's the USS Munsee.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Munsee. Okay.

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: ATF-107, I believe.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh. Very good. Anything else you can think of?

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: No. No.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You think that covers it?

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: I think that covers it. There's people often ask me, "Well, how come your family isn't so close?"

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: Isn't close, you know. If it's close -- how can you get close to your family when you're gone for practically 20 years, a year at a time away from anybody in the family. And then you can't get very close. You're gone too long to be close. I was pretty alone. I never went with -- with the family too much.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you get a lot of letters while you were on the ships?

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: No, I didn't get too much letters. My folks were immigrants and my father couldn't speak English. He could speak a little bit of English. Couldn't write English. But Mom wrote once in a while. But my sisters would write once in a while. But that's about it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: They didn't do much communicating.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: So they'd say, "What do you do, you know?" For all the time that you're away, you know, you can't be close to anyone. You don't make friends for long. You stay on a ship for four years, two years, a year, or whatever, month, couple months, and you're off again somewhere else. And they say, "Well, you get paid for it." Yeah, we got paid peanuts.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh. Well, very good. You think that covers it then?

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: I think it covers it. If I have anything that I can think of, I can call you back.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Okay. Good.

sp.speaker: John Medynski
sp.p: All right, sir. END OF INTERVIEW
